text: Deep Learning. Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers to learn increasingly abstract representations of data. It has driven recent progress in computer vision, speech recognition and natural language processing. Neural Networks. A neural network is built from layers of artificial neurons. Each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias, and passes the result through a nonlinear activation function such as ReLU, sigmoid or tanh. Without nonlinear activations, a stack of layers would collapse into a single linear transformation and could not model complex patterns. Backpropagation and Gradient Descent. Backpropagation is the algorithm used to train neural networks. It first performs a forward pass to compute the predictions and the loss, then applies the chain rule of calculus to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, moving backward from the output layer to the input layer. Gradient descent then updates each weight by subtracting the gradient multiplied by the learning rate. Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from small random mini-batches, which is faster and noisier than using the full dataset. Adam is a popular optimizer that adapts the learning rate for each parameter. Dropout and Batch Normalization.

Adam is a popular optimizer that adapts the learning rate for each parameter. Dropout and Batch Normalization. Dropout is a regularization technique that randomly sets a fraction of neuron outputs to zero during each training step. This prevents neurons from co-adapting and reduces overfitting. At test time dropout is turned off. Batch normalization normalizes the inputs of a layer across the mini-batch, which stabilizes and speeds up training. Convolutional Neural Networks. A convolutional neural network (CNN) is designed for grid-like data such as images. Convolutional layers slide small learned filters across the image to detect local patterns such as edges and textures. Pooling layers downsample the feature maps, which reduces computation and gives some translation invariance. Early layers detect simple features, and deeper layers combine them into complex shapes and objects. CNNs share weights across positions, so they need far fewer parameters than fully connected networks. Recurrent Neural Networks. A recurrent neural network (RNN) is designed for sequential data such as text, speech and time series. It keeps a hidden state that is updated at every time step, so information from earlier inputs can influence later outputs.

It keeps a hidden state that is updated at every time step, so information from earlier inputs can influence later outputs. Plain RNNs struggle with long sequences because of vanishing gradients. LSTM and GRU networks add gates that control what information is kept or forgotten, which lets them learn longer dependencies. RNNs process tokens one at a time, which makes them hard to parallelize. CNN versus RNN. CNNs exploit spatial structure and process the whole input in parallel, which makes them the standard choice for images. RNNs exploit temporal order and process input step by step, which makes them suited to sequences. Transformers have largely replaced RNNs for language tasks.

Machine Learning Basics. Machine learning is a field of artificial intelligence in which algorithms learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed with rules. A model is trained on examples and is then used to make predictions on new, unseen data. Supervised Learning. Supervised learning trains a model on labeled data, where every training example comes with the correct output. The goal is to learn a mapping from inputs to outputs. Classification predicts a discrete category, such as whether an email is spam. Regression predicts a continuous value, such as the price of a house. Common supervised algorithms include linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, support vector machines and neural networks. The main advantage of supervised learning is that its performance is easy to measure, because predictions can be compared directly with the known labels. Its main disadvantage is the cost of collecting and labeling large datasets. Unsupervised Learning. Unsupervised learning works with unlabeled data and tries to discover hidden structure on its own. Clustering groups similar examples together, as in k-means, which assigns each point to the nearest of k cluster centers. Dimensionality reduction, for example principal component analysis (PCA), compresses data into fewer features while keeping most of the variation.

Dimensionality reduction, for example principal component analysis (PCA), compresses data into fewer features while keeping most of the variation. Unsupervised methods are used for customer segmentation, anomaly detection and exploratory analysis. Reinforcement Learning. In reinforcement learning an agent interacts with an environment, takes actions and receives rewards or penalties. The agent learns a policy that maximizes the total cumulative reward over time. Reinforcement learning has been used to train game-playing systems and to control robots. Overfitting and Regularization. Overfitting happens when a model memorizes the training data, including its noise, and therefore performs poorly on new data. A typical sign is very low training error combined with high validation error. Underfitting is the opposite problem: the model is too simple to capture the pattern. Overfitting can be reduced by collecting more data, using a simpler model, applying regularization, using early stopping, or using cross-validation to choose hyperparameters. L2 regularization adds a penalty proportional to the squared size of the weights to the loss function, which discourages large weights. Evaluating Models. Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct, but it is misleading when classes are imbalanced.

Evaluating Models. Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct, but it is misleading when classes are imbalanced. Precision is the fraction of predicted positives that are truly positive. Recall is the fraction of actual positives that the model finds. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Data is usually split into training, validation and test sets; the test set is used only once, at the end, to estimate real-world performance.

Natural Language Processing and Transformers. Natural language processing (NLP) is the field of building systems that understand and generate human language. Typical tasks include text classification, machine translation, question answering, summarization and named entity recognition. Tokenization and Embeddings. Tokenization splits text into units called tokens. Modern models use subword tokenization such as WordPiece or byte-pair encoding, so a rare word is broken into smaller pieces and the vocabulary stays manageable. Each token is then mapped to an embedding, a dense vector of numbers. Word2Vec and GloVe produce one fixed vector per word, so the word "bank" gets the same vector in "river bank" and in "bank account". Contextual embeddings from models such as BERT produce a different vector for each occurrence, depending on the surrounding words. Self-Attention. Self-attention lets every token in a sequence look at every other token and decide how much each one matters. Each token is projected into three vectors: a query, a key and a value. The attention weight between two tokens is the scaled dot product of the query of one and the key of the other, passed through a softmax.

The attention weight between two tokens is the scaled dot product of the query of one and the key of the other, passed through a softmax. The output for a token is the weighted sum of the value vectors. Because attention has no built-in notion of order, positional encodings are added to the embeddings so the model knows where each token sits in the sequence. Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel so the model can capture different kinds of relationships. The Transformer Architecture. The Transformer was introduced in the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need". It stacks layers that combine multi-head self-attention with a feed-forward network, wrapped with residual connections and layer normalization. Unlike RNNs, a Transformer processes all tokens of a sequence in parallel, which makes training much faster on GPUs and allows models to scale to billions of parameters. The original design has an encoder that reads the input and a decoder that generates the output. BERT, T5 and GPT. BERT is an encoder-only model. It is pretrained with masked language modeling, where random tokens are hidden and the model must predict them from both left and right context.

BERT is an encoder-only model. It is pretrained with masked language modeling, where random tokens are hidden and the model must predict them from both left and right context. This makes BERT well suited to classification and retrieval. GPT models are decoder-only and are trained to predict the next token, which makes them natural text generators. T5 is an encoder-decoder model that treats every task as text-to-text. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines a retriever with a language model. Documents are split into chunks, and each chunk is converted into an embedding and stored in a vector index such as FAISS. At question time the question is embedded, the most similar chunks are retrieved by cosine similarity, and they are placed in the prompt so the language model can answer from them. RAG reduces hallucination because the answer is grounded in retrieved text, and it lets a system use private or up-to-date documents without retraining the model. A cross-encoder reranker can re-score the retrieved chunks by reading the question and each chunk together, which improves the ordering at the cost of extra computation. Chunk Size.

A cross-encoder reranker can re-score the retrieved chunks by reading the question and each chunk together, which improves the ordering at the cost of extra computation. Chunk Size. Chunk size is a trade-off. Small chunks make retrieval precise but may lose the surrounding context needed to answer. Large chunks keep more context but mix unrelated topics into one embedding, which blurs the match with the question. Overlap between consecutive chunks reduces the chance that an answer is cut in half at a boundary.
